1.2: One place, one painting

AS91913 v4 · Level 1 · 5 credits · Internal assessment · Painting focus

A flexible teaching unit leading to one substantial, resolved painting about a personally meaningful place. These original plans extend the student task sheet with teacher preparation, timed activities and checks for learning.

How to use the sequence

Twelve lesson plans of 50 minutes each. Repeat Lessons 8 and 10 with fresh goals to provide sustained painting time, and revisit preparation or reviews when needed. At three lessons a week, 24–30 sessions allows around 8–10 weeks: the twelve plans plus 12–18 additional studio sessions. Adjust to your timetable, students and the scope of the work.

Place the midpoint review after a meaningful period of production. Leave Lessons 11 and 12 until the work is ready; add studio time rather than reduce the substantial scope to fit a fixed lesson count.

Teaching route · repeat studio sessions as needed

The Painting Room · 1.2 · Unit overview 1 of 2

Prepare the unit

Before the first lesson

Confirm the current standard, exemplars, local assessment conditions, dates and authenticity procedures. Agree available materials, drying and storage space, and accessible source-gathering options. Plan a suitable water-based painting approach and follow school studio procedures.

Materials across the unit

Drawing books, pencils, scrap paper and viewfinders; student-made photographs and observations; approved acrylic or watercolour, brushes, palettes, water pots and rags; trial surfaces and agreed final paper or board; permitted artist references; a way to date progress records. Photography and projection are optional: prepare references in advance for an offline class.

Artist connections

Choose relevant works from the existing artist directory. Investigate Gossage’s relationship to place, Maughan’s constructed garden spaces or Sherald’s figure–ground decisions. Read the linked context with the works. Students apply a useful method to their own imagery; references are not templates or student exemplars.

  • Star Gossage · The Arts Foundation Te Tumu Toi · artist profile
  • Karl Maughan · Gow Langsford · artist profile and garden paintings
  • Amy Sherald · National Museum of Women in the Arts · artist and painting

Respect tikanga, permissions and the distinct contexts of Māori artists. Students need not disclose personal or cultural information; a school view or ordinary objects can offer an accessible starting point.

Assessment and teaching boundaries

The assessment focus is the substantial final artwork. Source studies, tests and progress records help learning and authenticity; quantities of trials, reflections and lessons are teaching suggestions. Use official criteria for judgements: suitable conventions at Achievement, consistent media management at Merit and skilful handling at Excellence. Do not turn the plans into a response template or a grade checklist.

Model processes on separate material. Adapt assistance to local conditions and approved access arrangements. Students choose their subject, composition, methods and revisions. Keep normal internal moderation and assessment records.

Primary assessment references

  • NZQA AS91913 · achievement standard (PDF)
  • NZQA AS91913 · annotated exemplars

Standard checked 22 November 2026. Confirm current guidance before assessment. Independent teaching resources; not NZQA-approved assessments.

Lesson 1: Find a place and a story

Visual Arts 1.2 · AS91913 v4 · 50 minutes · Teacher plan

Teacher / class: Date:

Learning intention

Choose a personally meaningful place and an idea a painting could communicate.

Students are learning to

  • Name a place you can observe or document yourself.
  • Connect a specific visual detail to an idea or narrative.

Materials & preparation

Set out drawing books, pencils and plain paper. Bring your own example of a familiar place and a short story about it. Prepare a classroom still-life or window view for students who need an accessible starting point.

Language to make visible

Idea / narrative · context · observation

Support & access

Offer a school-based place, a small selection of ordinary objects, sentence starters and oral recording. Personal disclosure is optional.

Extend the learning

Ask how the same place could communicate two different ideas through viewpoint or omission.

Class adjustments

The Painting Room · 1.2 · Lesson 1 · Teaching brief 1 of 2

Lesson 1: classroom sequence

Find a place and a story · 50 minutes, including clean-up

Lesson 1 timed teaching sequence
Time / phaseTeaching and learning
0–5 minConnectAsk students to list three places they know well. In pairs, describe one sound, object or memory connected to a place.
5–13 minTeach & modelModel moving from “the beach” to a specific intention: a worn path and empty seat might communicate returning or absence. Show how two viewpoints suggest different meanings.
13–38 minStudio practiceStudents choose a place, sketch two remembered details and write or orally record an intention. Arrange access to their own photographs or direct observation before Lesson 2. Offer the school grounds as an in-class option.
38–45 minReview & checkPairs point to one drawn detail and explain its connection to the intention. Confer with students whose idea is still only a topic; ask what they want a viewer to notice or feel.
45–50 minRecord & clean upCollect an intention and a source-gathering plan. Label books, return materials and check that any visit or photography follows school procedures.

Check for learning

A place, an initial intention and a feasible plan to gather original visual sources.

Before the next lesson

Check source access and permissions. Provide time in school for anyone unable to gather sources elsewhere.

Teacher reflection / next steps

Lesson 2: Observe and gather your own imagery

Visual Arts 1.2 · AS91913 v4 · 50 minutes · Teacher plan

Teacher / class: Date:

Learning intention

Gather first-hand visual information that can sustain a painting.

Students are learning to

  • Record distinctive shapes, tones and textures from your own source.
  • Choose imagery that helps communicate your intention.

Materials & preparation

Have pencils, viewfinders made from scrap card and drawing paper ready. Students bring their own photographs or observe an accessible school view or arranged objects. Check permission before photographing people or restricted places.

Language to make visible

Viewpoint · cropping · tone · primary source

Support & access

Use a nearby still-life, a viewfinder and large-format drawing tools. Allow verbal observations alongside drawing.

Extend the learning

Compare an unusual crop with a wider view. Explain how each changes the narrative.

Class adjustments

The Painting Room · 1.2 · Lesson 2 · Teaching brief 1 of 2

Lesson 2: classroom sequence

Observe and gather your own imagery · 50 minutes, including clean-up

Lesson 2 timed teaching sequence
Time / phaseTeaching and learning
0–5 minConnectStudents show a source or identify the classroom view they will use. Ask: what makes this particular place recognisable to you?
5–13 minTeach & modelDemonstrate looking before drawing: block in large shapes, compare light and dark, then select a meaningful detail. Use a viewfinder to change the crop without tracing an existing artwork.
13–38 minStudio practiceStudents make a broad tonal observation and a close detail study. They may take their own reference photographs where permitted. Ask them to record where and when the sources were made and select a useful viewpoint.
38–45 minReview & checkStudents compare sources against their intention. Ask which visual information is still missing and how they can obtain it. Check that reference images are their own or appropriately sourced for local assessment conditions.
45–50 minRecord & clean upPhotograph or collect the studies, label sources and clean the work area. Each student records one gap to fill.

Check for learning

Original source imagery and observation studies showing useful visual information.

Before the next lesson

Identify students needing more observation time. Select artist references relevant to the places and intentions emerging.

Teacher reflection / next steps

The Painting Room · 1.2 · Lesson 2 · Classroom sequence 2 of 2

Lesson 3: Learn from painting conventions

Visual Arts 1.2 · AS91913 v4 · 50 minutes · Teacher plan

Teacher / class: Date:

Learning intention

Identify painting conventions in context and test a method using your own subject.

Students are learning to

  • Describe a specific pictorial or material choice in a referenced artwork.
  • Try that method using your own imagery and acknowledge the artist.

Materials & preparation

Open the linked artist sources in the unit overview or prepare permitted reference material in advance. Select two relevant works with artist, title and context available. Set out water-based paint, brushes and small paper.

Language to make visible

Convention · pictorial space · edge · palette

Support & access

Provide a short vocabulary list and model one technique at a time. Discuss orally before writing.

Extend the learning

Compare two methods and justify which better communicates the intention, using the trials as evidence.

Class adjustments

The Painting Room · 1.2 · Lesson 3 · Teaching brief 1 of 2

Lesson 3: classroom sequence

Learn from painting conventions · 50 minutes, including clean-up

Lesson 3 timed teaching sequence
Time / phaseTeaching and learning
0–5 minConnectShow a selected work. Give quiet looking time, then ask what students can point to as evidence of how it was made.
5–13 minTeach & modelCompare a specific decision in each work: spatial structure, edges, colour relationships or paint layers. Read the artists’ contexts alongside the images; distinguish learning a method from copying their subject or culturally significant imagery.
13–38 minStudio practiceStudents choose one useful convention and make two small painted trials from their own source. They label the artist, source and method tested, then note how that method could serve their own intention.
38–45 minReview & checkPartners identify the tested convention from the painted evidence. Ask: what did you change to make the method appropriate to your subject?
45–50 minRecord & clean upKeep and label the trials, wash brushes and clear palettes. Record a convention worth investigating further.

Check for learning

Acknowledged artist references and painted trials that apply a relevant convention.

Before the next lesson

Check that methods and references suit each student’s intention. Revisit context or attribution where necessary.

Teacher reflection / next steps

The Painting Room · 1.2 · Lesson 3 · Classroom sequence 2 of 2

Lesson 4: Test colour and paint handling

Visual Arts 1.2 · AS91913 v4 · 50 minutes · Teacher plan

Teacher / class: Date:

Learning intention

Choose paint processes and colour relationships that support your idea.

Students are learning to

  • Mix and repeat useful colours with increasing control.
  • Explain how a material choice affects the mood or meaning.

Materials & preparation

Provide school-approved acrylic or watercolour, suitable paper, water pots, rags and a limited set of colours. Prepare a dry sample to show layering. Keep wet trials separate from books until dry.

Language to make visible

Hue · value · opacity · layering · consistency

Support & access

Limit the palette, offer larger brushes or adapted grips and use a single source detail. Provide a dry example to handle and inspect.

Extend the learning

Keep a consistent value structure while changing temperature; compare the effect on atmosphere.

Class adjustments

The Painting Room · 1.2 · Lesson 4 · Teaching brief 1 of 2

Lesson 4: classroom sequence

Test colour and paint handling · 50 minutes, including clean-up

Lesson 4 timed teaching sequence
Time / phaseTeaching and learning
0–5 minConnectStudents choose a trial from Lesson 3 and name one technical problem they need to solve.
5–13 minTeach & modelDemonstrate a light-to-dark colour range, appropriate paint consistency and a hard and soft edge. Show how to clean a brush between mixtures. Connect the demonstration to a real passage in your own example.
13–38 minStudio practiceStudents make a small palette test, then paint the same source detail in two ways. Change one variable such as value range, opacity or edge. Label mixtures or processes so a useful effect can be repeated.
38–45 minReview & checkStudents place trials beside their source. Ask which treatment best supports their intention and whether they can reproduce it. Offer a focused reteach to students struggling with paint consistency.
45–50 minRecord & clean upStore wet tests flat, clean equipment and record a useful mixture or process.

Check for learning

A repeatable palette or handling test and a reason for the selected approach.

Before the next lesson

Allow additional practice where paint handling is still preventing the intended effect. Keep successful recipes available.

Teacher reflection / next steps

The Painting Room · 1.2 · Lesson 4 · Classroom sequence 2 of 2

Lesson 5: Compose the painting

Visual Arts 1.2 · AS91913 v4 · 50 minutes · Teacher plan

Teacher / class: Date:

Learning intention

Develop and select a composition that communicates your intention.

Students are learning to

  • Compare genuinely different arrangements of your own imagery.
  • Explain how placement, scale and tonal structure guide attention.

Materials & preparation

Provide source studies, paper, pencils and paint for a small colour study. Bring a viewfinder and an example showing how a changed crop alters a composition.

Language to make visible

Composition · focal area · negative space · tonal structure

Support & access

Use movable paper shapes derived from the student’s own drawings and a limited tonal range. Let students explain their selection orally.

Extend the learning

Develop an unexpected arrangement and test whether it communicates the idea more clearly than the first choice.

Class adjustments

The Painting Room · 1.2 · Lesson 5 · Teaching brief 1 of 2

Lesson 5: classroom sequence

Compose the painting · 50 minutes, including clean-up

Lesson 5 timed teaching sequence
Time / phaseTeaching and learning
0–5 minConnectAsk students to describe where they want a viewer to look first and why that matters to their idea.
5–13 minTeach & modelDemonstrate several quick arrangements of the same source: change crop, overlap, scale or empty space. Reduce one arrangement to three tones to check its structure.
13–38 minStudio practiceStudents make several small alternatives, then develop a promising arrangement in tone or limited colour. They compare it against the intention and retain an alternative rather than choosing only the neatest sketch.
38–45 minReview & checkPairs describe the viewing path before hearing the artist’s explanation. Students use that feedback to select or revise their proposal.
45–50 minRecord & clean upLabel the selected plan and keep alternatives. Clear materials and record the next technical question.

Check for learning

Composition alternatives and a reasoned selection linked to the idea.

Before the next lesson

Check that the selected composition offers enough depth for a substantial painting and that students have the sources they need.

Teacher reflection / next steps

Lesson 6: Agree the scope and production plan

Visual Arts 1.2 · AS91913 v4 · 50 minutes · Teacher plan

Teacher / class: Date:

Learning intention

Plan a substantial single painting with suitable scale, depth and technical finish.

Students are learning to

  • Explain how the proposed painting will communicate the idea at its chosen scale.
  • Plan practical stages and test a demanding passage.

Materials & preparation

Prepare available supports, rulers and sample surfaces. Set out the current student task sheet, standard and exemplars for teacher reference. Have a simple calendar of available studio sessions and drying or storage constraints.

Language to make visible

Scale · depth · technical finish · production

Support & access

Provide a planning checklist and break the production into manageable stages. Adapt tools or support without removing the necessary scope.

Extend the learning

Ask students to justify a consequential choice of surface or scale through a comparison test.

Class adjustments

The Painting Room · 1.2 · Lesson 6 · Teaching brief 1 of 2

Lesson 6: classroom sequence

Agree the scope and production plan · 50 minutes, including clean-up

Lesson 6 timed teaching sequence
Time / phaseTeaching and learning
0–5 minConnectStudents show their selected composition and identify the part most likely to be technically difficult.
5–13 minTeach & modelExplain how scale, complexity, production time and finish work together. A large support alone does not establish substantial scope. Model a short production plan and testing a passage at the intended working scale.
13–38 minStudio practiceStudents test a challenging passage and draft a proposal: intention, conventions, support, scale, materials and stages. Hold short conferences to agree a feasible scope and enough production time; students retain ownership of choices.
38–45 minReview & checkStudents check the proposal against their actual tests. Ask what must be practised or adjusted before committing to the final support.
45–50 minRecord & clean upRecord agreed materials and the next stage. Store tests and return equipment. Schedule further planning where the proposal needs development.

Check for learning

An agreed substantial scope, a production plan and a relevant working-scale test.

Before the next lesson

Confirm readiness individually. Extend preparation rather than requiring everyone to start the final work on the same day.

Teacher reflection / next steps

The Painting Room · 1.2 · Lesson 6 · Classroom sequence 2 of 2

Lesson 7: Prepare the surface and block in

Visual Arts 1.2 · AS91913 v4 · 50 minutes · Teacher plan

Teacher / class: Date:

Learning intention

Establish a sound surface and the main structure of the final painting.

Students are learning to

  • Prepare a support appropriate to the chosen medium.
  • Establish the main forms and tonal relationships from the selected plan.

Materials & preparation

Have agreed supports, approved grounds if needed, brushes, sources and plans ready. Prepare surfaces in advance if drying exceeds the lesson. Allocate named drying and storage spaces; follow school procedures for all media.

Language to make visible

Support · ground · underpainting · block-in

Support & access

Use enlarged student-made plans, accessible tools and a brief individual check of the main forms. Demonstrate on separate material.

Extend the learning

Test whether an underlayer can contribute to the intended atmosphere rather than simply cover the support.

Class adjustments

The Painting Room · 1.2 · Lesson 7 · Teaching brief 1 of 2

Lesson 7: classroom sequence

Prepare the surface and block in · 50 minutes, including clean-up

Lesson 7 timed teaching sequence
Time / phaseTeaching and learning
0–5 minConnectStudents check their plan and surface. Ask what preparation this material needs before paint is added.
5–13 minTeach & modelDemonstrate the relevant surface preparation on a separate sample. Show how to locate large shapes and tonal masses without committing too early to small detail.
13–38 minStudio practiceStudents prepare or use a pre-prepared support, establish the composition and block in major relationships. Pause halfway to compare the painting with the intention and plan. Students decide whether any proportions or placements need changing.
38–45 minReview & checkView work from a distance. Students identify whether the main structure is legible and select one adjustment before further development.
45–50 minRecord & clean upTake a dated progress photograph where appropriate, record the next stage, clean tools and store work safely.

Check for learning

A prepared support and a purposeful beginning of the single final painting.

Before the next lesson

Repeat or extend this stage when preparation or drying needs it. Resolve structural problems before adding detail.

Teacher reflection / next steps

Lesson 8: Build the painting relationships

Visual Arts 1.2 · AS91913 v4 · 50 minutes · Teacher plan

Teacher / class: Date:

Learning intention

Develop the painting while maintaining consistent colour, space and paint handling.

Students are learning to

  • Connect a working decision to the intention and selected conventions.
  • Manage paint handling across connected areas of the painting.

Materials & preparation

Return dry paintings, source material, successful tests and mixing notes. Prepare the agreed media and a separate demonstration surface. Allow students to be at different production stages.

Language to make visible

Relationship · consistency · focal area · layering

Support & access

Agree one achievable goal, provide a visual sequence for tool use and offer a short technique recap on separate material.

Extend the learning

Ask students to sustain the same quality of handling through a less successful passage, rather than adding more detail to a strong one.

Class adjustments

The Painting Room · 1.2 · Lesson 8 · Teaching brief 1 of 2

Lesson 8: classroom sequence

Build the painting relationships · 50 minutes, including clean-up

Lesson 8 timed teaching sequence
Time / phaseTeaching and learning
0–5 minConnectStudents inspect the whole painting and set one specific studio goal, pointing to the passage they will work on.
5–13 minTeach & modelDemonstrate a shared technical need identified in the class, such as joining adjacent colours or layering over a dry passage. Keep the example separate from student work and connect it to the effect it produces.
13–38 minStudio practiceStudents develop connected areas using their tests and plan. Prompt regular distance checks. Confer through questions: what is happening here, what effect are you seeking, and which option will you test? Record progress without prescribing solutions.
38–45 minReview & checkStudents compare the beginning and end of the session. Ask what changed in the painting and whether the change supports the intention. Identify any issue needing a fresh trial.
45–50 minRecord & clean upRecord a short next-step note, photograph progress when useful, clean and store work. Keep mixtures or process notes for continuity.

Check for learning

Visible progress in the final painting and an identifiable student-led decision.

Before the next lesson

Repeat this studio plan with a new student-set goal as needed. Reserve a midpoint review before the work becomes too settled.

Teacher reflection / next steps

The Painting Room · 1.2 · Lesson 8 · Classroom sequence 2 of 2

Lesson 9: Review the painting at midpoint

Visual Arts 1.2 · AS91913 v4 · 50 minutes · Teacher plan

Teacher / class: Date:

Learning intention

Use evidence from the painting to decide what needs strengthening.

Students are learning to

  • Describe what the painting currently communicates.
  • Choose and test a revision that addresses a visible issue.

Materials & preparation

Arrange space to view paintings upright and from a distance. Return intentions, source studies and dated progress images. Have scrap paper or spare supports ready for tests before changes to the final painting.

Language to make visible

Critique · intention · evidence · revision

Support & access

Use a small feedback group, descriptive sentence starters and oral or recorded responses. Keep feedback focused on one visible issue.

Extend the learning

Invite a revision that strengthens relationships across the whole composition rather than repairing an isolated detail.

Class adjustments

The Painting Room · 1.2 · Lesson 9 · Teaching brief 1 of 2

Lesson 9: classroom sequence

Review the painting at midpoint · 50 minutes, including clean-up

Lesson 9 timed teaching sequence
Time / phaseTeaching and learning
0–5 minConnectAsk students to look at their painting silently and note where the intended idea is most and least clear.
5–13 minTeach & modelModel descriptive feedback: “I notice … because …” followed by a question. Separate observations from preferences. Show how a small trial can help evaluate a possible revision.
13–38 minStudio practicePairs or small groups describe what they see before hearing the intention. Each artist selects an issue, tests a possible change on spare material or in a study, then decides whether to apply it. Hold brief individual conferences.
38–45 minReview & checkStudents point to the test and explain the decision. Ask whether the proposed change addresses the issue identified, and what evidence would show that it worked.
45–50 minRecord & clean upKeep a dated before-and-after record or review note, then clean and store the work.

Check for learning

A focused review, a relevant test and a decision grounded in the painting.

Before the next lesson

Plan further studio sessions from the review. Redirect unfinished technical learning to a separate trial before continuing.

Teacher reflection / next steps

The Painting Room · 1.2 · Lesson 9 · Classroom sequence 2 of 2

Lesson 10: Resolve a demanding passage

Visual Arts 1.2 · AS91913 v4 · 50 minutes · Teacher plan

Teacher / class: Date:

Learning intention

Strengthen technical command where the painting needs it most.

Students are learning to

  • Identify a specific handling problem and practise a useful solution.
  • Apply a selected process consistently in the final work.

Materials & preparation

Review midpoint notes and group students by technical need where useful. Set out spare supports, chosen media, dry samples and each student’s successful tests. Prepare a focused demonstration based on observed needs.

Language to make visible

Control · fluency · transition · surface

Support & access

Reduce simultaneous technical demands and provide adapted tools or a short process card. Reteach on separate material.

Extend the learning

Ask students to vary handling intentionally while preserving coherence and the clarity of their idea.

Class adjustments

The Painting Room · 1.2 · Lesson 10 · Teaching brief 1 of 2

Lesson 10: classroom sequence

Resolve a demanding passage · 50 minutes, including clean-up

Lesson 10 timed teaching sequence
Time / phaseTeaching and learning
0–5 minConnectStudents point to a demanding passage and describe the intended effect rather than simply saying it needs to be “better”.
5–13 minTeach & modelDemonstrate one relevant process on a separate surface: a tonal transition, an intentional edge, controlled layering or a repeated brush mark. Discuss the decisions and material conditions that make the effect repeatable.
13–38 minStudio practiceStudents practise their selected process, compare the trial with the intended effect and apply it when ready. Encourage checks across adjoining passages so the technique supports the whole painting.
38–45 minReview & checkStudents compare the revised passage with a related area. Ask whether the handling is consistent and what remains unresolved. Avoid treating a technique exercise as a substitute for the final artwork.
45–50 minRecord & clean upKeep a useful trial, record the next priority, clean equipment and store paintings.

Check for learning

An improved passage that contributes to consistent handling in the final painting.

Before the next lesson

Repeat this lesson or Lesson 8 with a fresh goal until the painting is ready for whole-work resolution. Adjust the schedule individually.

Teacher reflection / next steps

The Painting Room · 1.2 · Lesson 10 · Classroom sequence 2 of 2

Lesson 11: Unify and finish the painting

Visual Arts 1.2 · AS91913 v4 · 50 minutes · Teacher plan

Teacher / class: Date:

Learning intention

Bring the painting to a coherent technical and communicative resolution.

Students are learning to

  • Review the whole painting against the intention and chosen conventions.
  • Make purposeful finishing decisions and recognise when to stop.

Materials & preparation

Provide upright viewing space, suitable lighting, clean brushes and agreed media. Return intentions and progress records. Check drying time before the presentation lesson; plan extra studio time where necessary.

Language to make visible

Resolution · unity · technical finish · coherence

Support & access

Use a whole-work review checklist and help students order tasks without choosing their pictorial solutions.

Extend the learning

Ask how restraint, selective emphasis or a final subtle adjustment could clarify the idea more effectively than added detail.

Class adjustments

The Painting Room · 1.2 · Lesson 11 · Teaching brief 1 of 2

Lesson 11: classroom sequence

Unify and finish the painting · 50 minutes, including clean-up

Lesson 11 timed teaching sequence
Time / phaseTeaching and learning
0–5 minConnectStudents stand back and identify the most distracting unresolved relationship in the painting.
5–13 minTeach & modelModel a whole-work review on separate material: composition, colour relationships, edges, surface and focal emphasis. Discuss when a change strengthens the work and when further detail might weaken it.
13–38 minStudio practiceStudents prioritise a small set of finishing decisions and work through them. Pause for distance checks and compare the effect with the intention. Use neutral conferencing questions; the student decides the final changes.
38–45 minReview & checkStudents explain whether the work is resolved and identify the evidence. Agree further production time if the substantial artwork remains unfinished.
45–50 minRecord & clean upRecord final decisions, check safe storage and drying, clean tools and arrange the next presentation stage.

Check for learning

A single substantial painting approaching or reaching a coherent finish.

Before the next lesson

Do not force a final declaration for an unresolved work. Confirm readiness and local assessment dates before presentation.

Teacher reflection / next steps

The Painting Room · 1.2 · Lesson 11 · Classroom sequence 2 of 2

Lesson 12: Present, reflect and review evidence

Visual Arts 1.2 · AS91913 v4 · 50 minutes · Teacher plan

Teacher / class: Date:

Learning intention

Present the resolved painting and explain the decisions that communicate its idea.

Students are learning to

  • Present the single painting with its title and clear identification.
  • Use visible evidence to explain selected conventions and technical decisions.

Materials & preparation

Prepare a dry, safe display space and photography setup if used. Confirm the school’s evidence, authenticity and moderation procedures. Bring process records and the student task sheet; gather reflection responses without imposing an extra assessment threshold.

Language to make visible

Presentation · reflection · authenticity · acknowledgement

Support & access

Offer an oral reflection or scribed access arrangement where appropriate. Use a clear presentation checklist and accessible viewing options.

Extend the learning

Compare the starting intention with the final painting and explain how a significant decision changed the communicated meaning.

Class adjustments

The Painting Room · 1.2 · Lesson 12 · Teaching brief 1 of 2

Lesson 12: classroom sequence

Present, reflect and review evidence · 50 minutes, including clean-up

Lesson 12 timed teaching sequence
Time / phaseTeaching and learning
0–5 minConnectStudents check that their work is dry, identified and ready to be viewed. Revisit the initial intention.
5–13 minTeach & modelModel a concise reflection that points to a particular painted passage, names a technical choice and explains its contribution. Clarify the locally agreed presentation and source-acknowledgement process.
13–38 minStudio practiceStudents title and present the single painting, document it as required locally and prepare a short written or oral reflection. Keep sources and progress studies available to support process and authenticity. View peers’ work respectfully.
38–45 minReview & checkStudents share one choice that communicates the idea and one future learning goal. Teacher checks completeness and authentic process; make assessment judgements separately against the official standard and normal moderation procedures.
45–50 minRecord & clean upCollect or record the agreed evidence, return resources and leave display and storage areas ready for the next class.

Check for learning

The final resolved painting, with locally agreed identification and supporting process records available.

Before the next lesson

Assess the substantial final artwork holistically. Use current NZQA guidance to calibrate judgements; reflect on teaching needs for the next unit.
